utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness, I've asked to be found. I couldn't find him this morning. I don't know which room he's in at the moment. He's going to testify in open session and won't require any pseudonym. While he's being brought in, can I make use of the time to mention two points about witnesses. I hope to conclude this witness, that is, Veton Surroi, today and tomorrow, leaving enough time tomorrow for at least one 92 bis witness. I hope it may be more, but at least one. And I'm going to have to take a 92 bis witness out of order. Number 3 of that list, Latifi Rahim or Rahim Latifi has I think final Ph.D. exams or something similar. I'm not quite sure what it is. I beg your pardon, Number 4, Zhafer Beqiraj and he has final Ph.D. exams for Monday. He's made every effort, I understand, to have the examiners to adjust their timetable but it hasn't been possible for them to do so and therefore, he simply has to go home on Saturday. Sorry. Not number 3, number 4, Xhafer Beqiraj. The second witness timetable issue relates to Ambassador Vollebaek, who is serving ambassador to the United States, of Norway. He was originally scheduled to come here and came here during the period of time when the accused was unwell. He then reorganised his diary to come next Tuesday and, of course, next Tuesday was then identified as a day when the Court could not be sitting. He's looked at his diary again. He can come on the 8th and 9th of July but on no other day, and given his position and the accommodations he's already made for us, I hope that Monday and Tuesday will be days when his evidence may be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Towards, one hopes, the very end of your case on this part of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As for the other witness, clearly his evidence must be heard tomorrow. We should make every effort to hear this witness's evidence today and tomorrow. Of course it will partly depend on you, Mr. Nice, and how quickly you can get through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I intend to deal with the summary wherever possible by yes/no answers wherever possible and to deal with it if I possibly can in two sessions which will therefore leave the accused two sessions, if he requires them, for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And there seems to be evidence about earlier events. I think those are matters which you can probably leave out unless they're really essential. Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following on from Your Honours' last observation, I shall be dealing with background matters and in particular, although I understand the Court's made some observation about education, with education, but from a particular point of view, because they are relevant, but I will deal with them all, wherever possible, in summary and Mr. Surroi will, I think, understand that. I should also lead unless -- on matters that are non-contentious, to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But first can you give us, yourself, your full name.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: My name is Veton Surroi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are a Kosovo Albanian, the son of a diplomat, having lived in Bolivia and Mexico, also briefly in London, an educated man, speaking several languages, and by occupation a journalist and publisher; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your first work as a journalist was with the newspaper Rilindja?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Between 1982 and 1990. As a result of something you published there, were you -- or did you lose that job?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: That's correct. They stopped me from writing for a year in my own newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This, I think, was following the publication of an article or an interview, indeed, with a Croat intellectual, Branko Horvat, who observed that Kosovo should be a republic within Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That I haven't checked.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please speak up and into the microphone the interpreter requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's working. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, you've been asked by the interpreters over the headphones, which you do not need to use, to speak up and into the microphone. I think that that same newspaper was, on a date in 1990, closed and reopened under a management board of Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. With the establishment of emergency measures in Kosova at large, when not only Rilindja but the Prishtina radio and television were also closed down and the Assembly was suspended and all the other institutions of the Kosovar Albanian autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you start a weekly news magazine in September 1990, being its publisher and editor-in-chief, and if so, can you give us its name so we can pronounce it correctly?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. Its name was Koha, and it was the first Albanian weekly, independent Albanian weekly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1991, was there a period of shutdown of the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The Koha newspaper had been registered in Croatia, which was one of the two Yugoslav republics where private newspapers could be registered. The beginning of the war between Serbia and Croatia made it impossible for the publication and distribution of the Koha newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it restarted publishing in what year?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: First of all, following an impediment towards its registration by Serbia, which lasted for about six months, it re-emerged in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it then shut down again later on, and if so, in what year and, in a sentence, in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: After publishing a photo montage called Anschluss 1989, which showed the accused, the security, the state security organs encircled the publishing house and stopped the distribution of the newspaper in the month of April 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to the staff and the building?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The state security personnel, the Serbian state security personnel questioned some of the members of the staff, inquiring about the methodology of the operation of its staff, the eventual responsibility of the people who contributed to the newspaper was the printing press was closed down and sealed up with a state security -- with a state security seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did this event draw any international attention? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that subsequent to a series of protests at the state -- state security organs in Serbia and organisations of the free speech in particular, this case fell into oblivion and the newspaper was allowed to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 6. Did Koha become a daily paper as the Koha Ditore in April 1997? I beg your pardon. There became a daily newspaper and then you had a magazine and a daily newspaper.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. That very same year, a daily appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were the proprietor of both?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The editorial policy of your titles being what? Paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: We always attempted to have an independent or a policy that would be critical and also professional and open to all sources of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, if any, identifiable attitude did you take to the party of Ibrahim Rugova?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I've been critical, especially towards the manner of the reality being represented, which would represent almost half of the truth. But I've also tried to represent the attitudes and political stance of the party and Mr. Rugova in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In particular, did Mr. Rugova and his party hold and express views about the future of Kosovo and its independence?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Rugova personally, and his information apparatus, gave the impression that the question of the independence of Kosova was a matter of days, and that the entire international community was dealing on a daily basis with the question of Kosova. Over a critical period, for instance, prior to the Dayton talks, the Democratic League of Kosovo apparatus was basically going about saying the question of Kosova would be solved, resolved at Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that an attitude that your newspapers espoused as realistic or were you critical of it?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: We clearly pointed out, based on several sources, that this was an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. aberration of reality, this was. And it was our own professional duty to inform Kosova's citizens as to where Kosova lay, the occupied Kosova lay, Kosova that was occupied by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, so that on these general matters we can see how this affected your standing and the way you were viewed, were you regarded, as a result of the attitude of your paper, as being particularly anti-Serbian or not?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: We've clearly been against the Serbian regime, power regime, and fascist ideology, whilst at the same time being open to the views of Serbian citizens who enunciated liberal opposition attitudes. At the same time, we were the only newspaper to break the taboo, the only Albanian newspaper to break the taboo by beginning to refer to the independent news agency Beta, as a result of which, extremist circles, on several occasions, accused us of representing Belgrade's platform and Belgrade's information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to other events concerning the newspapers a little later, but now travel quickly over the same period of time, just touching on your own political activities. For one way and another, you've been involved in political activities or politics all your life. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, I do see myself as an activist of civil society.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm sure you'll bear in mind that we must keep the politics to the relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The danger is if there is too much politics discussed, the trial gets sidetracked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm indeed aware of that, and I was going to touch on this witness's background just for context and arguably for reasons of credibility should any aspect of his evidence be challenged by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position is this, Mr. Surroi: You've set out or there's been set out for you in the summary how you wrote articles for the Croatian press which were critical, how you were a participating member of the Yugoslav democratic initiatives, UJDI, as long as 1989, which was a movement for the democratisation of Yugoslavia represented throughout the former Yugoslavia; is that correct? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You helped form the first trade union for construction workers in 1989; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were involved in the parliamentary youth movement from 1990 to 1992, but you then resigned from that as a defined political organisation, and I think thereafter revealed your interest in politics in other ways.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you can tell, if anybody wants to know about it, in detail of demonstrations, including those you had a part in organising; for example, the candle demonstration in February of 1990, which was a demonstration over the killing of some 30 people in previous demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1991, you were known as a person who had organised anti-war or violence protests called the Burial of the Violent Day and, as a result of that, you were imprisoned for 60 days, initially, where you served only two? D

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Much later, paragraph 15 - and we'll hear about this when we come to your meetings involving the accused - there was a demonstration following the massacre at Prekaz in 1998, and as a result of your involvement in that demonstration, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I was beaten up by a number of Serb policemen as I was protesting whilst sitting on a Prishtina street, and I suffered injuries in my arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to deal not in a way that's actually set out in the summary but in much more general terms with something to do with education. The Chamber's already heard quite a lot of the history of the education agreement, so we can deal with it with you very swiftly as a history, but could you please explain in a few sentences why it is that education for Kosovo was an important issue in a way that it might not be for other Western countries and therefore not be readily understood by those who do not have Kosovo experience?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The Albanian people in Kosova was almost totally illiterate at the end of World War II. This is part of an old heritage amongst the Albanians, given to the fact that the first unified Albanian alphabet dates back to 1908; i.e., very late. Secondly, the heritage of the Yugoslav kingdom meant that there were no Albanian schools allowed to open. There were two fundamental factors: First the overwhelming need of a people to get education in its mother tongue; and secondly, demographics. Albanians are the youngest people in Europe, therefore, there's a greater number of people growing up and needing education than in other Western countries. And at a time when Albanian schools in Kosova were being shut down, that is, following the years 1989, 1990, every fourth Albanian citizen in Kosova was tied, in one way or another, to the educational process, be it as a student or a teacher. The -- and in the political growth of the Albanian people in Kosova, with the expansion of the autonomy, was closely linked to the increased -- to its increased capabilities to get educated, which led up to the university and the profound enhancement of studies therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the significance of education to Kosovo Albanians something that was readily recognised and understood by others, for example, those in government elsewhere in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It was clear that part of the conflict between the anti-Albanian ideology in Serbia and the Kosova Albanians centred on the education, and the persistent efforts to curtail Albanian education finally erupted after the abrogation of the autonomy and manifested itself in the shutting down of Albanian schools as a form of stopping the growth of the Albanian people in Kosova and its maturation as a state-forming subject -- political subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are only three exhibits with this witness. One, please; K2408. This is a Security Council report of the 24th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 101.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 17, in the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, you've reviewed this document, I think.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you care to comment on the contents of the Kosovo passage, starting at paragraph 47 concerning -- education is mentioned there, but just do so very briefly because it's document of record that we can then refer to.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The document in question reflects the political attitude that we took at that time and which was that because the question of Kosova's political status was a difficult one to solve, the question of the status should not obstruct the right of the citizens of Kosova to receive education in their mother tongue. And from that time, it was the Albanian political -- politicians insisted always in a peaceful manner on agreement and on involving the international community on solving an extraordinarily difficult problem, which was education, which affected the great majority of the citizens of Kosova. So in 1991 and 1992, which this document is concerned with, we tried -- we tried at international conferences, at meetings with international politicians to create a way of opening schools in some way despite the unsolved nature of the Kosova question. This was part of our policies of -- in a peaceful manner and through dialogue of solving everyday social problems while leaving the question of status for a time when conditions would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, with those general observations in mind with this document of record to which we may refer, we can now go to paragraph 18 but simply pass through history because the Chamber's already heard of it from other witnesses. There was the education agreement brokered by Sant' Egidio in September 1996, which you understood from other sources was signed and eventually announced but not implemented.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To make the point -- no. I beg your pardon. It wasn't implemented, in summary, for what reason?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that the Sant' Egidio agreement was in fact exploited in order to create a block in the negotiating process in which the negotiation process would lose its impetus and -- on the Albanian side, while the entire problem of Kosova would be concentrated on the question of whether one school or another would be opened or not. In fact, the agreement and the delays in implementing it was a tactic to delay a solution of the Kosova question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 22. At about the same time as the agreement was being made, were there demonstrations concerning electoral practices?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: These were the demonstrations after the agreement, and these were in Belgrade. And these had to do with local elections which the opposition parties called electoral theft. And this led to a sense of outrage among the citizens of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any consequences of those demonstrations you would want to refer to or comment on?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that the weakness or the response of the opposition in Belgrade led to a crackdown by the state apparatus. And in fact, also in some cases at the beginning of the 1990s, as long -- until the war to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. confrontation. The confrontation between the Serbian regime and the opposition was reflected later in the war that began in Croatia. For us in Kosova, the deterioration of internal relations between the government and the opposition in Serbia was a signal to us that the moment was coming when the Serbian regime would -- would -- would distract public attention towards Kosova because this was a nationalist ploy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next series of negotiations on which you can give, if asked, some personal assistance of the Bertelsmann Science Foundation talks, which occurred in autumn of 1996 and into 1997; correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the course of these talks which happened in Rhodos in Greece and I think elsewhere, but you had contact with a political party run at the time by the Serbian Minister of Internal Affairs, Dusan Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This is the present Interior Minister, Dusan Mihajlovic. At that time, he was part of the civic alliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you've listed others involved at that time in paragraph 23. How seriously were these negotiations taken, and in a sentence, what was their result? And we can produce a document that deals with it and then move on.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There were three basic issues. First, we all believed that a track 2 for negotiations had been opened. And second track negotiations did not involve members of the government, but nevertheless, the readiness to negotiate would be conveyed to them. Secondly, at this meeting, we participants from Kosova showed our readiness to start on a new way towards approaching a solution of the Kosova issue of not confronting the issue of the status, a question which should come at the end, but to create a framework of administering a kind of peaceful process that would, on the one hand, lead towards improved living conditions, and secondly, would lead to discussions of -- about the end of these negotiations which could be approached without prejudice. Thirdly, we conveyed to both sides the fear that the -- the lack of negotiating process would lead to war, would lead to a deterioration of the situation because this situation would be unstable over a long period of time. So we insisted at all costs on avoiding war and finding a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second exhibit of this witness, K2824.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the second meeting was in Halki in Greece; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In Munich and then in Halki.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a five-page document dated --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 102.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dated 1997 from Halki. The Joint Recommendations, we can read it at our leisure, but we can see on the first page, third paragraph under Joint Recommendations for Resolution, an observation that comprehensive democratisation of Serbia is necessary but not a sufficient precondition for reconciliation, and further observations on what is required. And over the page, under Confidence Building and Practical Improvements, "The education agreement of September 1996 should be implemented without further delay." And an explanation of what would be required. Was this document, and we can see, scanning our eyes over it, other topics covered such as disarmament on 3 at paragraph 5(e). Is this document one that, in your judgement, fairly represented the then-positions?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This is a document that reflected the way in which the issue could be solved, and it reflected a fair range of the scope of the debate, and of course, both the Albanian and the Serbian sides had opposite attitudes towards this document, but nevertheless, the document represented the degree of consensus that might have been achieved at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just, I think, a couple more questions about this negotiation process. Paragraph 27, you've mentioned Mihajlovic, and there are others - Tanic and Simic - who were involved. What was their position on the probabilities of maintaining the status quo in Albania at that time -- in Kosovo at that time?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: All the Serbian participants took the view that the status quo could not be maintained, and they warned of a wave of violence, and they were all, without exception, against this wave of violence that was being prepared and which they themselves were sensitive of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And they were signed up to, they were in agreement with this document that we've looked at, for their part?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, the promise was that this attitude would be conveyed to the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that brings me to the last question, last two questions on the topic. The Serbian authority of the accused and his party, had they participated in these talks themselves at all?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: We have information that one of the participants, who was one of the members of the government coalition, obliquely conveyed the position of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you name that person or not?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic represented the New Democracy Party, which was a part of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then finally on this topic, did you understand whether a copy of the document we've now looked at in brief was passed to the accused or not?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: According to the information that was given to me personally by the Bertelsmann Foundation, this document was part -- was given to German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel in Belgrade, and there, with two participants in the meeting, it was handed over to the Serbian authorities, including the accused himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were in due course, as we shall hear, to participate at Rambouillet. The attitude of the Albanian, Kosovo Albanian negotiators at the Bertelsmann meetings was it, in your judgement, consistent with or inconsistent with the line taken subsequently at Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think it was consistent in the sense that we insisted on finding a framework of self-administration which would leave the question of Kosova's status open. But the question of Kosova's status would not be prejudged in advance and -- but everyday -- everyday issues had to be solved first, and first an administrative framework had to be found which would not pre-judge Kosova's political status and then we could talk about the question of status. All the efforts of the Rambouillet delegation were concentrated on stopping the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to Rambouillet in a few minutes. For completeness, passing over or passing through paragraphs 29 and 30, was there a further series of talks or couple of talks called the Project on Ethnic Relations which happened in Belgrade in 1997? Did you have some part in those, including in the second meeting in New York?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I took part in both meetings. In the first meeting in Belgrade, there was Professor Agani and myself. And later, the Albanian participants were broadened. And in this first meeting at Belgrade, one of the members of the leadership of the Serbian Socialist Party, Mr. Pecvic, a member of the ruling party, was also present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the event, did these meetings come to anything?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think they showed two things. First, they showed the readiness of the Albanians of Kosova to -- to insist on a peaceful solution. And second, they showed that they -- there was a great gulf between the Albanians' attitude and the attitude of the Serbian regime. And indeed, to some extent, the standpoint of the Serbian opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next in order -- it may not be in chronological order but it probably is, an offer to mediate by a man called Pacolli but that didn't come to anything?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: As far as I know, as the late Professor Agani told me, a businessman who had ties with the Serbian regime and the accused offered his services as a mediator, but this offer was immediately refused by Professor Agani.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then come to events of which the Chamber has already heard from another witness, and that is the meetings involving Mr. Bakalli and the DB. You weren't involved in those yourself. Did you hear anything about them?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I was informed about these meetings only after they were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you informed of any threats about what would happen to villages in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The mediator at these meetings was a member of my staff, and he told me that the results of the meeting with the state security head, Stanisic, was a direct threat that if a solution were not found between Belgrade and Prishtina, the Serbian regime had identified ethnically pure villages that would be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that, in the climate in which you were operating, something that was taken seriously or something that could be shrugged off as mere words?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Knowing where these words came from, we took them very seriously. At that time, we had the impression that Stanisic was a trusted person of the accused and his message to us was a very serious one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So when later you learned of the dismissal of Stanisic and Perisic, how did you interpret what was happening then?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: For me, it was a surprise. And bearing in mind the standpoint, the rather milder standpoint taken by General Perisic, who at that time had a rather less confrontational tone and was inclined to avoid confrontation, the dismissal of these two members of the government's inner circle could have been interpreted as an omen of war or of a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. deteriorating situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now for the reference of the Chamber, at paragraph 35, I only want to focus on the title of this paragraph. You don't have it in front of you but there's a paragraph in your summary headed "Koha Ditore role during the war and Jashari attacks." Now, the war, which war are you speaking of? More important so that we can understand your terms of reference, when did it start?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that the war started -- started with the attacks on Prekaz and the massacres of the Jashari family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the date of that was?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The first siege in Drenica was in January; the end of 1997 and the beginning of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember the date of the killings?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What role did your newspaper have in relation to those events and to what degree did it become involved with people from around the world?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: At that time, our newspaper was the only one that reported from the scenes of events. And what our reporters saw was a major massacre under preparation. And there was the Deliaj family and the Jashari family, and people were being executed in front of their own homes. And because this attracted international attention to the cases, we opened our offices to all the diplomats and the correspondents from foreign countries in order to urgently convey an alarm and to sound the alarm in the world that a war was under way against the citizens of Kosova, against the Albanians of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then have heard already of the formation of something called the G15. Was the United States diplomat Gelbard involved at this time as well?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Mr. Gelbard was very much involved, especially in the idea that the Albanians of Kosova should form a negotiating team that would urgently enter into negotiations with the Belgrade regime. And as a result of this atmosphere that had been created, the G15 negotiating group was formed, and this was supposed to represent the broad spectrum of Kosova opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were a participating member.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I was a member of the G15 group as an independent member.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Gelbard particularly significant in persuading Mr. Rugova what attitude he should take in relation to the work of G15?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Gelbard was a key figure in persuading Rugova that a broad spectrum of people should be represented in this negotiating group, especially in a situation in which Mr. Rugova believed that he had been elected the President of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shortly after the formation of this group, was there some concern about the apparent absence of international mediation in the crisis, and did Ambassador Holbrooke then take a role?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: For us, it was a sine qua non condition that there should be international mediation in the negotiations with Belgrade. Not only did we not trust the sincerity of the opposite side, but we had been -- we had been inured to ten years of failed negotiations with Yugoslavia, and we thought that international mediation was a key factor in their success. And this trust was further reinforced when the referendum in Serbia was organised against involving international mediation. And at this moment, the statement by Ambassador Holbrooke was decisive, and by the very fact of going to Belgrade and to Prishtina and arranging a forthcoming negotiating process, he showed not only that international mediation was possible but also vital and productive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You speak of the organisation or is it arrangement of the referendum on international involvement. Probably obvious, but just tell us, which way did the vote -- which way did the vote go?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The voting led to an overwhelming majority against international mediation after what I would call a very intense propaganda on the part of the government's side against international involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We go now to the meeting with the accused of the G5 group, of which you were a member, some of the evidence having being given unchallenged thus far. The meeting involved Mr. Rugova, Fehmi Agani, Mahmut Bakalli, Pajazit Nushi, and yourself.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think there was some concern, paragraph 40 of your summary, about Mr. Rugova's ability to meet on his own and it was thought preferable to go in as a group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I was surprised at the announcement of the news that Mr. Rugova would meet with Mr. Milosevic, and together with Professor Agani and Mr. Bakalli, we decided that it would be difficult, from a moral point of view, to meet the accused whom we considered to be responsible for crimes in Kosova and, nevertheless, we shouldn't leave Mr. Rugova alone, because we had doubts in his competence to conduct a fruitful meeting with the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You set out your -- or there are set out in your summary other concerns you had about -- reflecting the wishes of Ambassador Holbrooke, but let's not be under any illusions. G5 and G15 had what as their ultimate goal, so far as Kosovo's independence was concerned?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There was this consensus among the Albanians of Kosova, which was reflected in the G15 and G5 group, and this was that the status of Kosova should be a matter for self-determination by its people, i.e., the independence of Kosova for which the people of Kosova had already spoken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The meeting was on the 15th of May at the White Palace, as we have already heard. Is this the first time, or the only time that you met the accused?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This was the only time that I met the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to take you through the various, in a sense, domestic details of the meeting. You can tell us about them if they become relevant and if you're asked. But at the stage of greetings between the accused and the members of the G5, was there any indication that he'd met any of them before, from things that were said?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I didn't have the impression, and I was surprised by the closeness and the warmth with which the accused greeted members of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just yes or no to this, if you wouldn't mind. So far as you were concerned, was the business of meeting the accused one that presented issues, including moral issues, for yourself?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When it came for you to have a chance to contribute to the discussion, can you tell us, please - paragraph 44 - what you covered and how the accused responded?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that the most important part of this intervention, on my part, was about the violence and the massacre of the Jashari family. When I raised the question of the massacre of the Jashari family, the witness [as interpreted] interrupted me, saying that it would be insane to think that the Serbian police would kill children. And then he started to say how Adem Jashari was a criminal and so forth and that he had killed his family. I said, "Then why? In this case, why isn't it allowed for a team, an international team from a neutral country to come, an international forensics team, that would come to investigate how the Jashari family had died? And if they were killed by a shoot-out among themselves, then this would exculpate the Serbian forces from any responsibility. And on the other hand, if the opposite were proved, then a process to identify who was responsible could be begun."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the transcript has, and as interpreted, the witness as saying that it was the "witness" who interrupted. Yes, perhaps you could just clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've heard what His Honour said, Mr. Surroi. Whether accurately translated or not, the transcript has you saying that it was the witness who interrupted you. Who was it who said it would be insane to think that the Serbs would kill children?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It was the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The proposition that Jashari had killed his own family, coming to you from the accused, is that something that you heard before this day in all your dealings?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I had heard it, this interpretation, from the spokesman of the Serbian forces and from the Serbian media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any other support that you as a journalist had ever found for it anywhere else, apart from those particular sources?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No, nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused having given you this version of events and you having proposed the use of an international investigative team, what was the accused's reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: He only said, after an expression of annoyance, "We'll see," and then he looked at his secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How well-informed in detail did the accused appear to be about this event?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I had the impression that he was very well-informed because he explained to us details, according to his own interpretation, of how the operation had been conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he have or refer to any notes or was he speaking from memory or knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: He didn't have anything written. He spoke very fluently, and I had the impression that he was persuaded of the truth of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's cover a couple of other topics at this meeting. Was anything said by any of the delegation about education, and if so, can you, in summary, say what the accused's attitude to that was? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Mr. Agani in particular, because he was responsible for the signing of the Sant' Egidio agreement, raised the question of education as one of the issues which were also raised by the accused. Mr. Agani said it was quite incomprehensible how the implementation had been so late in being applied. And the accused, at the end of the meeting or at the end of this part of the meeting, said how the Serbian parliament was in the course of preparing a law on education which, according to him, would deal with certain issues and would make it possible to implement the agreement more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was anything said about the university?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It seems to me that the key words were about the university, because the Serbian rector of the university had obstructed the implementation of the agreement. And as we heard later as part of the purges that followed the law being prepared by the Serbian politics -- parliament, after purges at Belgrade University involving the dismissal of opposition teaching staff who disagreed with the regime, the rector of the Serbian regime in Prishtina was also involved and was dismissed. And then the -- the process of the share-out of university premises for Albanian students and Serbian students started to go faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were, of course, a newspaper publisher. Anything said about that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: At one point, the accused, trying to describe the climate in which he lived, he accused me of being a dictator [as interpreted] and said to me, "Mr. Surroi, has your newspaper ever been closed?" And he said -- he said this with a smile, and I said, "Yes, you have closed it." And he was surprised to hear this and said, "When?" And I said, "When I published a photo montage. But that's not the greatest problem today. The greatest problem today is violence and war, armed conflict."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another small translation problem. Who accused whom of being a dictator, according to the accused?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The accused was talking about public opinion, and he hadn't pinned down anybody in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was speaking of other people accusing him?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The transcript had it wrong. And finally, did the question of Kosovo's status come up explicitly? If not, was it touched on by the accused at all?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The question of the status of Kosova was mentioned at the beginning of our meeting by Mr. Rugova, and he said that the citizens of Kosova -- and we were determined on independence, but then we passed to another subject and the accused did not pay any attention to this issue and didn't address the question of Kosova's status.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But at the end of the meeting, was anything said by him, if not about independence, about nationalists or nationalism?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. He did mention in particular whilst referring to pressure or what he described as internal pressures, he said, "Look, I've got my own nationalists," i.e. nationalists that do create problems for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of interest, when you left the meeting, were you optimistic, pessimistic or about the same? We can see from the end of paragraph 41 how you really approached the accused, but how did you leave the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I concluded that the gap dividing us was huge and I foresaw difficult days ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused himself, his approach and manner throughout the meeting at that -- you haven't described it but you can, and did that change your view of him at all? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The accused was someone who established quick relations with the interlocutors, tried to create an easy-going atmosphere, in fact, wanted to insert a motif of sympathy in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you returned from the meeting to Pristina, what in fact happened, as far as food imports were concerned?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: A few kilometres before the border between Kosova and Serbia, where a Serbian checkpoint was set up, we noticed a large convoy of lorries transporting different sorts of goods, and subsequently learned that in fact a blockade, a food blockade on Kosova had started. And these were the first results of this blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any explanation given from Serbia as to what triggered this blockade?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I'm not exactly aware of the interpretation, but as far as we were concerned, this was an unusual coincidence, which means that at a time when we were supposed to talk on how to resolve the problems, new problems appeared to crop up. We agreed that this was an act of pressure towards Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there change in military activity in the immediately following days?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: During that month, that is to say, during the month of May, the -- a huge operation of clearing up the border belt started, including in particular the Decani area. And towards the end of that month and the beginning of June, we faced an increased number of refugees, many of whom remained holed up -- up in the mountains on the border between Kosova and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any explanation given publicly for the particular timing of this operation and the consequential increase in number of refugees?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There was no explanation given with the exception of the official explanation that these were anti-terrorist activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The meeting with the accused had been intended the first of a series of bilateral meetings involving G15; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. And another meeting over the following week was announced between our own negotiating team and the team that had been appointed by the accused, who actually included members of the Serbian government and the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That second meeting occurred. Do you remember the date? Don't guess it if you don't.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: A week later. It had been planned for the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The -- it was held, I think, in the offices of the LDK in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can list those present, if necessary, or just identify them from time to time, but -- in your evidence, but did the group you were facing appear to have any power to make decisions by themselves?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I'm of the opinion that these came from the inner circle, as was the case of Nikola Sainovic or Ratko Markovic, but I think that in every single negotiating situation, they had no decision-making powers but only the right to consult, and the decision-making remaining with the man they considered to be their superior, their boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, what appeared to you to be the purpose from their side of this meeting; negotiation or something else?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I did not detect a great deal of readiness to negotiate, even though a number of issues were put on the table, it was more a matter of form rather than content. For instance, we spent more than half an hour debating where to hold the next meeting. Whether it would be held in Belgrade, as we insisted, in order to set in motion a circle of such meetings in Belgrade, or at the government buildings in Prishtina, as they insisted, to create the impression that these were talks within -- held within the same region that were dealing with local issues which necessitate a local handling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there ever a third meeting held?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, because this was also difficult to do, but also -- but also there was increased international pressure on us, in particular by Ambassador Holbrooke, to participate in this meeting. The situation, however, was deteriorating rapidly. And in lieu of creating a better atmosphere towards negotiation, we were heading increasingly into -- into more violence and open problems. We therefore insisted within the negotiating group that it would be futile to hold negotiations when the situation kept deteriorating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you, the members of the G5, how had you been described at home in respect of your going to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There was many kinds of reaction, many of them unpleasant. Many of the labelling was unpleasant. Two of the members of the G15 resigned at the very moment when we decided to go to Belgrade regarding that if not some kind of treason, something bordering on treason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By this time, what number was put on internally displaced Albanians in the mountainous regions?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: In May and the beginning of June, we faced a huge crisis. There were around 5.000 civilians who, given that snow had not melted yet, were hiding atop mountains on the border between Albania and Kosova with no food, no clothes, no heating; nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think Sadako Ogata was eventually involved, head of UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: We alarmed the American mediator Chris Hill, who had been accepted by the Belgrade side too. We told him that this was a huge humanitarian crisis in the vicinity or in the environs of Decani and, given that UNHCR staff were not allowed to travel at that stage, we contacted directly Mrs. Ogata so that she would intervene and be able to send humanitarian relief to the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the -- there were people killed in Ljubenic, as we've heard -- we haven't yet heard, on the 25th of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. It was prior to our meeting with President Clinton, the meeting of four members from Kosova. This was one of the signals on -- bespeaking a red line of execution of civilians in front of their own homes. This was one of the incidents demonstrating the continuity of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. police and military activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following that, there was the Serbian university law that you've already told us about, initially presented by the accused in the meeting as being what? Something of a positive step?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. He announced that there'd be a law which would clear up some of the matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the end, was it a positive step or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think it brought a good deal of damage to education in -- to the university in Serbia, and in fact at the same time the problems had exacerbated to that extent in Kosova at the moment that it was almost irrelevant whether Rector Popovic would remain in his position or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then we come to the meeting with President Clinton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That may be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are obviously on target to finish the evidence in chief early in the next session, not within half the next session. So I hope the examination or cross-examination of the witness may indeed be concluded today. If the accused has very little to ask the witness, I will make arrangements -- were he minded so to express himself, I will make arrangements for some of the 92 bises to come here today, otherwise they will not, of course, be immediately in the building. We don't ask them to come here unless there is an expectation of their coming -- an expectation of their giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Surroi, we're going to adjourn for 20 minutes. Could you remember in this and any other adjournment there may be during these proceedings while you're giving evidence, not to talk to anybody about it until it's over. That includes members of the Prosecution. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Surroi, you went to Washington on days in May of 1998 for meetings with the US government, including with President Clinton.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... paragraph 64 and 65. What do you remember as the dates, please? And if you don't remember them, don't guess.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: It was May the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you met the President, of what did you inform him?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I informed President Clinton, taking the example of the massacre at Ljubenic, that regardless of our readiness to negotiate and obtain a peaceful solution, the Serbian regime is escalating the situation with new acts of violence and the killing of civilians. I requested that a security framework of circumstances be created which, with international mediation, would enable the beginning of negotiations. That in turn would set up a self-administration process whilst, at the same time, paving the ground, the way for the status which remains or remained the biggest confrontational issue between Prishtina and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were your talks known of by others, including the accused?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think the contents of the talks would be known with the exception of the members of the talks. Yes. The meeting had been publicly announced throughout the world media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what happened when you emerged onto the White House lawn with President Clinton? What did you discover?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: At that moment, as we emerged from the White House, we got information from activists who had contacts with Prishtina, and then through my contacts with my staff that the situation had further escalated around Pec and Decan and that political and military activity had increased and the number of refugees had risen dramatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any particular reason given for the escalation? Any cause that you could identify?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that everybody on the Kosovar side that took part in that meeting considered this a response on the part of Belgrade towards our talks with President Clinton. This was a way of telling us that if you meet the American President, this is what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We return to Rambouillet in February 1999. In your summary, there is set out a number of not anecdotal but in a sense small-scale events that we needn't weary the transcript with and the Judges with unless it's strictly necessary, but tell us this: What view did you eventually form about how conscientious, how serious the Serbian delegation was?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that a great number of people within this delegation weren't even aware of why they were there. And with the exception of three or four people who came from the circle, the inner circle, they just wasted their time. In the first two weeks of negotiations at Rambouillet, we also noticed that even this inner circle had not come there to negotiate but to obstruct the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your side, the Albanian side, was it taking these negotiations seriously?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Absolutely. It was vital for us. It was not only the issue of the present but the future was at stake as well. And we undertook those negotiations under very difficult circumstances in which, first of all, we had to keep in mind that we were temporarily giving up on the status of independence; i.e., these were not talks which would bring independence which was an aspiration of everyone's. And secondly, within the framework of these negotiations, we had to seek a way of dismantling the KLA, the Kosovo Liberation Army, which was a difficult issue, given that guerilla forces are difficult to persuade, to transform into civilian life. This is a difficult procedure in every other country where guerrilla movements do exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had there been an understanding either, at arrival at Rambouillet or before, as to the authority that would be vested in the negotiation groups and as to whether those groups would be seeking authority or direction from outside?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: There was an agreement, a total agreement which we had reached with the mediators that the delegations would be fully empowered to make decisions. And there was the preliminary agreement that we would not seek consultation with persons outside the Rambouillet castle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sainovic was one of the representatives on the Serb side. Did there come a time when he left the negotiations to go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I asked Ambassador Hill, who was one of the mediators, why members of the Belgrade delegation were being allowed to go to Belgrade, and he replied that Sainovic had asked to consult with the accused because in fact it would be the accused who would make decisions. And according to Ambassador Hill, this might be -- this might help the negotiation process because the negotiations were more or less paralysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The consequence of Sainovic leaving the talks included what, so far as your delegation was concerned?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: One member of our delegation, Mr. Thaci, asked as a response that he, too, should go and meet with Mr. Demaci. And according to the mediators, in order to create the necessary equivalence, the balance, this was allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, those talks ended. The Paris talks in March occurred. On the Serb side, President Milan Milutinovic was one of the participants. What was his apparent authority?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: He was -- he introduced himself as somebody who could assist the Belgrade delegation. But nevertheless, at a certain moment -- at the final moment, when it came to signing the agreement, according to the three international mediators, that is Majovski, Ambassador Hill, and Petric, he said that in fact his boss in Belgrade would have to make the decision and he could do nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we'll move on from those talks. But without leaving the month of March of 1999, tell us, please, what happened to your newspaper at about the same time as the Paris talks.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Because we were late in getting back from Paris because we were not allowed to land at Prishtina airport, I was a day late, and when I arrived on a Sunday in Prishtina, I had heard previously that the Serbian authorities had -- had prosecuted the newspaper Koha Ditore for publishing a report by a Western news agency which had quoted Hashim Thaci, who had accused the Serbian authorities of destroying Albanian villages. According to the repressive Serbian media law which had been adopted by the Serbian authorities, this law punished any newspaper that presented facts which, according to the government's interpretation, were not true. And in an exceptional judgement taken on a Sunday, at which Bajram Kelmendi and Hasmi Bali were lawyers involved, we were fined a large sum. And if we did not pay this fine, we would be closed down. And after three days, the NATO bombing started, so that the newspaper was in fact closed not because of this law but because, on the night of the bombing, uniformed police entered the editorial office, killed our guard Rexhep Ramadani, and then either confiscated or destroyed all the equipment we had. One night later, our printing works was burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you ever known of your local courts sitting on a Sunday before?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: This was entirely extraordinary, not only in Prishtina, but I have never heard of such cases anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last, we come to the NATO bombing, and just a few matters arising from that. I'm not sure you told us in your account of what had happened who your lawyer was. I don't think you did. Oh, yes you did; Bajram Kelmendi. Tell us what happened to Bajram Kelmendi, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Our lawyer was Bajram Kelmendi, and that Sunday afternoon we had a last meeting, and on the night of the bombing, a few hours after the bombing started, at his home, according to what his wife and brother-in-law said, they were taken by uniformed police, Bajram and his two sons were taken and taken to an unknown place and executed. On the morning of the 25th, his -- Bajram's brother-in-law told me that the police had taken the men of this family. And I phoned Bajram's wife, Nekibe, and confirmed this. Later, I heard that Bajram and -- they had taken the bodies of Bajram and his brother-in-law, and I heard that they had been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And for what type of legal work was Bajram Kelmendi well-known?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Bajram was a human rights -- a defender of human rights par excellence. He was one of the founders of the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms, and he had been a defence lawyer in almost all the political trials. He had defended me personally several times, whether in my capacity as a newspaper editor or as an organiser of protests which were called the "Burial of Violence."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a few final matters on the last page of the summary. The general attitude of the Albanian population to the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Although most of us were opponents of violence, the bombing, the first bombings and the later bombings were welcomed with what I might call relief and even joy. They were indeed bombs aimed at a regime that had invaded us and enslaved us, and we thought and hoped, and as it turned out later, it turned out to be the case, that these bombs would bring us freedom. And none of us -- I do not think that any of us thought about the danger from the bombs because the Serbian soldiers, policemen, and paramilitaries were so very much more dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Rugova and his position, whether he was thought to be free or otherwise and thought to be exercising free decision during the bombing, what's the position on that?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that Dr. Rugova and some other people were in fact hostages of the regime. And his behaviour during the war and during the bombing, and his public statements and his various writings which rather look like a kind of quisling behaviour, can be interpreted only in -- as the behaviour of a person who is frightened for his own life and the life of his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that is the opinion of the witness. It is not of assistance to us with respect to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning to another issue which it may be difficult to distinguish your opinion from the facts, but do the best you can. We're looking at the history of Fehmi Agani, and very briefly his relationship to the KLA. How well respected or otherwise was Fehmi Agani amongst Albanians, Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Dr. Agani was a respected figure for the whole nation. And I can say that he was the sole figure within his party who was fully respected both by parties or movements that were somehow opposed or disagreed with his policies. I could say that Dr. Agani was a respected figure. And I saw this during the Rambouillet negotiations. He was respected by all of the participants in our delegation, including the members representing the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he have, apart from at these negotiations, meetings and contacts with the KLA from time to time?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Even before, in 1998, Dr. Agani had had contacts with various political representatives of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course when you say at Rambouillet, he was respected by all participants, it's notwithstanding the criticism you make of the Serbian delegation, do you include that delegation as those who appeared to have respect for him?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that Dr. Agani was respected as a trustworthy and balanced person even though he was -- there were -- there were -- I think he was respected even in Belgrade, even though there were clear differences of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As things worsened, was there an expectation that Agani would leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I had heard rumours that he was preparing to leave. I'd heard from a personal friend of his. And the situation that was created during the bombing posed a danger of recreating political problems between representatives of the KLA and the LDK and various political parties, and Rugova's appearance in Belgrade would exacerbate the situation further within -- among the Albanians of Kosova, and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is pure opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can I move to the next question, please, Mr. Surroi. What, in the event, happened to him?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I saw news on the Serbian television and on foreign television about the murder of Mr. Agani. He was executed. According to Serbian sources, he was executed by KLA forces. But what we learned later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Surroi, unless you've got some direct evidence about it, this is merely what you've heard, and we'll have direct evidence, no doubt, in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about his murder on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to trouble the Court with the third exhibit to which I made reference, which is a summary of Kosovo -- suffering by Kosovan violence to Albanians early in the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I would like your assistance on one other topic before I close. As a man who has travelled around the world as well as throughout the former Yugoslavia, can you assist the Chamber with how Kosovo Albanians were either regarded or dealt with, not just at home but, for example, when they were in Serbia? What status, what jobs they occupied. If you can summarise that position for us, please.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The overwhelming majority of Kosova Albanians in the former Yugoslavia, especially in Belgrade, were manual workers. And indeed, in the 1940s and 1950s, they were well-known as being woodcutters, and they knew that anybody carrying a saw would be an Albanian. And then they delivered coal to houses. And even in the Serbian dictionary, the daily vocabulary, people didn't say, "Go and fetch a worker to cut wood," but they said, "Go and find an Albanian to bring the coal." It had the same connotations of low value as -- as in California they say, "Go and fetch a Mexican to clean the yard." Or they might say in the south of Europe, in Spain or Italy or Greece, "You've got to find a Filipino to clean the house." It had this kind of association. They were identified with this kind of work that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And had that attitude changed significantly or at all by the time of the war with which you've been dealing?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: After 1968, Kosova started to develop, especially in education, with the creation of a new elite. And there was a conflict between this kind of identity of the new elite who were educated and the old conception of the Albanians as manual workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I ask. You may be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the son of a Yugoslav diplomat, practically all your life you spent -- you had a silver spoon in your mouth; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes, for a long period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Everything you achieved - we see this from your CV - was made possible for you by the Yugoslav society, starting from your material status all the way up to your education.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Yes. My parents catered for that. They were part of that society.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you were also part of that society together with your parents.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Up until the moment when that society was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I haven't received an interpretation. I did not hear an interpretation. I didn't hear any sound whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, ask another question and we'll see if it's interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So were you also part of that society?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Up until that society was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the social status, standard of living, freedoms, human freedoms, human rights, everything else that defines the quality of life was incomparably higher in Kosovo and Metohija than in the neighbouring Albanian state, the Republic of Albania?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Until the year 1990, yes, it was higher than in Albania and far lower than the rest of Yugoslavia, including Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is no contest to the effect that Kosovo was an underdeveloped part of Yugoslavia. That is why it was developed at an accelerated rate. However, you say that that was until 1990. Do you know, for example, that your friend Christopher Hill, who you've often been mentioning in your statement and who was there much later, both in Albania and in Kosovo, do you know that he told me how he felt when he would leave Albania and get into Kosovo? He said that he felt as if he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were entering Disneyland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That sounds like the opinion of Mr. Hill. You can ask him, if he's going to give evidence, about it. This witness can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking him whether he told him something to that effect or not, because we are talking about comparisons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we take into account comparisons, there are some regions of Bolivia which were so underdeveloped that when I returned from Bolivia into Kosova, Kosova appeared to me to be Utopia. I can't see how Albania enters into this equation vis-a-vis Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it gets into the equation because it is probably undeniable, as far as you are concerned too, that Kosovar Albanians, economically, politically, socially, from the point of view of their rights, were much better off in Kosovo than they were in Albania which was their own state. Isn't that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I grew up under the conviction that Kosova was my own state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You grew up under the conviction that Kosovo was some kind of an independent state?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I grew up with the conviction that Kosova was my fatherland, a part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As part of Yugoslavia, of course. As part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: As a part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you share the view, if you look at this historically, when the Albanians were under the Turks and under the Germans and under the Italians and under the Russians and now under the Americans, that practically only in Yugoslavia, only in Serbia - that is to say, in Kosovo and Metohija - that they were free and that they managed to develop freely and that that is why such progress had been made precisely in that area? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Albania -- excuse me, interpreter corrects, Kosova is only correct at this stage only because its citizens are free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, that's enough of a general debate. Let's get on to what the evidence was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A short while ago, Mr. Nice asked you how the Kosovo Albanians were viewed within Serbia and, for example, in Belgrade. You said that they were manual labourers, which is for the most part correct. It is certain that there were a great many Serbs who were manual labourers as well, as is the case until the present day. But do you know that there were physicians, university professors, depending on the level of education, a considerable number of Albanian intellectuals who also lived in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: I think that the proportions go greatly in the -- disfavourably towards the Albanians, and this disfavour has helped create a stereotype that obtains that when somebody wanted someone to cut wood before the winter, it was an Albanian he turned to. But I think that this stereotype has now been overcome or is in the process of being overcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you ascribe that to the level of education or to some national criteria?

utterances.speaker: VETON SURROI
utterances.text: The stereotypes are always a product of low cultural levels or lack of communication and ethnic distances or other identity distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that, for example, the Albanian language got its own alphabet only in 1908, and you also said how much the level of education lagged behind that of the other peoples in the Balkans.
